# Soochana — Odisha Demographic Intelligence Portal: Complete Data Book

_Generated on 17 November 2026 from the portal files (`data/`, `datasets/`, `excel/`, `learn/data/` and the data held in page scripts). Every number is copied from those files; each section names its file and its source. Where the portal shows NFHS-5, the NFHS-6 value (published May 2026) is given beside it._

## 1. Sources used in the portal

| Publication | Publisher | Date | What the portal uses it for | Portal files |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NFHS-6 (2023–24): India and State/UT Fact Sheets; State and District Fact Sheets, Odisha | International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) | Published May 2026 (Odisha fieldwork 18 July – 28 November 2024) | Latest round on every page: state and district health, nutrition, family planning, fertility, women’s empowerment | nfhs6_state_factsheet.json, nfhs_district_rounds.json, learn/data/districts.json, tectonics-s2.js |
| NFHS-5 (2019–21): State and District Fact Sheets, Odisha; India Report Volume I | IIPS and ICF; MoHFW | Fact sheets 2021; India Report Vol. I, March 2022 | Shown beside NFHS-6 as the earlier round; district life expectancy and mortality estimates | nfhs6_state_factsheet.json, nfhs_district_rounds.json, district_life_expectancy.json, district_mortality.json |
| NFHS-4 (2015–16) | IIPS and ICF; MoHFW | 2017 | Older round in district life expectancy, mortality and the Learn modelling table | district_life_expectancy.json, district_mortality.json, learn/data/districts.json |
| Population Projections for India and States 2011–2036 (Report of the Technical Group on Population Projections) | National Commission on Population, MoHFW (ORGI, Census 2011 base) | July 2020 | Odisha population, age structure, sex ratio, density, vital rates and state TFR to 2036; carries district figures to 2031 and 2036 | orgi_state_projection.json, state_demographics.json, hero_data.js, unfpa_district_projections.json |
| District Level Population Projections in Selected States of India – 2021 & 2026 | UNFPA India | 2022 | District population by age and sex, 2021 and 2026 (2031 and 2036 carried forward with the ORGI state ratios) | unfpa_district_projections.json, district_population_trends.json, district_age_pyramids.json, hero_data.js |
| South India Interstate Migration Survey 2026 (SIIMS 2026) | IIMAD (International Institute of Migration and Development), UNFPA and IOM | 2026 | Migration figures on the home page, the Tectonics migration story and the repository | home.js, tectonics-migration.html, repository.html |
| Census of India 1901–2011 | Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India | 1901–2011 (Census 2011: 2011–13) | Population history, literacy, density, urban and tribal share, sex ratio, administrative counts | state_demographics.json, district_population_trends.json, districts_detail.json, learn/data/districts.json |
| Sample Registration System (SRS): Statistical Report 2024; Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality 2022–24; Abridged Life Tables 2020–24 | Office of the Registrar General, India (ORGI) | 2024–2026 releases; district MMR 2017–19 | Birth rate, death rate, IMR, MMR, life expectancy on the home page; district MMR | data/key_stats.js, districts_detail.json |
| UDISE+ 2023–24 and 2024–25 | Department of School Education & Literacy, Ministry of Education | 2024, 2025 | District school statistics (dropout, transition, pupil–teacher ratio, smart classrooms, computers) | districts_detail.json, learn/data/districts.json, excel/ |
| Odisha Economic Survey 2025–26 (and 2024–25) and Government of Odisha district statistics | Planning & Convergence Department, Government of Odisha | 2025, 2026 | Economy, land use, rainfall, irrigation, roads, health infrastructure, banking | districts_detail.json, state_details.json, data/reports.json |
| Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) | National Statistics Office, MoSPI | Annual reports | Employment theme | excel/Employment.xlsx, data/reports.json |
| UN World Population Prospects 2024 | United Nations, DESA Population Division | 2024 | India comparison series on Parallel Journeys | journeys.html |

**Not used:** the earlier DIU Bayesian district fertility projections (`datasets/district_fertility_trends.json`) are retired and no page shows them. District fertility is shown from NFHS-6 and NFHS-5 instead; neither round publishes a district total fertility rate.

## 9. District population, 1951–2036

_Source: Census of India 1951-2011; UNFPA, District Level Population Projections in Selected States of India – 2021 & 2026 (published 2022); Population Projections for India and States 2011-2036, Technical Group, ORGI_

- District names follow the portal spellings (Angul, Bolangir, Boudh, Khordha, Nabarangpur).
- District age bands stop at 75+; the portal splits 75+ into 75-79 and 80+ in the ratio of the ORGI state projection.
- Male + female can differ from the total by a few persons because of rounding in the source.
- District totals for 2021 and 2026 sum to within 1,000 of the ORGI state total; the methods differ.
- Workbook sheet "Odisha PP" labels the 1991 male and female columns the wrong way round; this file takes 1991 from the district sheet, which is correct.
- State "under_1" is part of the 0-4 band and must not be added to it.

**Demography.** Odisha is well into its demographic transition: population growth is easing, families are smaller and people are living longer. The official projections put the population at 4.57 crore in 2021 and 4.90 crore in 2036, with growth slowing from 0.89% a year in 2011–21 to 0.32% a year in 2031–36. Fertility is below the replacement level: 1.7 children per woman in NFHS-6 (2023–24, published May 2026), from 1.8 in NFHS-5 (2019–21). The sex ratio is recovering from its low of 1991, from 979 women per 1,000 men in 2011 to a projected 987 in 2021 and 998 in 2036. The age structure is shifting with it: the working-age share stays close to 65% through 2036, the share of children eases from 23.6% in 2021 to 18.9%, and people aged 60 and over rise from 11.5% to 17.0%, from about 52 lakh to 84 lakh. With a large rural and tribal population, this change unfolds differently from district to district. The years ahead are an opening: a large working-age population to equip with skills and jobs, and time to build social protection and care for a growing number of elders.

**Health and nutrition.** Odisha's health profile shows steady gains in access to care. Births in a health facility reached 93.9% in NFHS-6 (2023–24, published May 2026), from 92.2% in NFHS-5 (2019–21). Households with health cover rose to 82.7% from 47.9%, mothers taking iron and folic acid for 100 days or more to 74.5% from 60.8%, and full vaccination of children aged 12–23 months holds at 90.8% (90.7% in NFHS-5). Stunting among children under five came down to 26.8% from 31.0%. The next areas of focus are care during pregnancy, where four or more antenatal visits stand at 73.6% against 78.1% in NFHS-5, and acute undernutrition, where wasting is 22.1% against 18.1% and underweight 31.6% against 29.7%. The NFHS-6 fact sheets do not report anaemia or mortality rates; for those, NFHS-5 (2019–21) remains the latest survey, and it recorded falling neonatal, infant and under-five mortality alongside rising anaemia among young children and pregnant women. An extensive primary care network gives the state a strong base to build on in maternal nutrition and micronutrient programmes.

**Education.** Odisha's education system is predominantly government-led, with strong access and progression through the foundational and middle stages. However, retention becomes a key challenge at the secondary level, where dropout rises notably despite relatively adequate teacher availability. Digital readiness is improving, although the spread of smart classrooms remains limited compared with basic computer access. A persistent gender gap in literacy further highlights unequal educational attainment, particularly for women. Overall, the state has established a strong foundation in school access and transition, but improving secondary-stage retention, digital learning infrastructure and gender equity remains critical to strengthening educational outcomes.

**Geography.** Odisha, on India's eastern coastline (155,707 sq km, ~480 km coastline on the Bay of Bengal), spans coastal plains, central plateaus, the Eastern Ghats and highlands (covering ~12% of the state), western rolling uplands, and major river flood plains, drained by the Mahanadi, Brahmani, Baitarani, Subarnarekha, Rushikulya, and Vansadhara. It borders West Bengal to the northeast, Jharkhand to the north, Chhattisgarh to the west, and Andhra Pradesh to the south.

**Tribal communities.** As per the Census 2011, Odisha has the third-highest percentage of tribal population in the country, which stands at 95,90,756. The state has 62 different tribal communities spread over 30 districts and 314 blocks. They constitute 22.85% of the state's total population and contribute 9.17% to the country's total tribal population.

**Demography.** Angul is undergoing a clear demographic transition, shaped by slowing population growth, declining fertility and a gradual shift towards an older age structure. With a population of about 12.74 lakh, a relatively low sex ratio of 943 females per 1,000 males, and an urban population share of 16.21%, the district remains predominantly rural while experiencing gradual urbanisation. Population projections indicate that growth will stabilise over the coming decades as the total fertility rate continues its sustained decline. At the same time, the share of children and young people is projected to shrink, while the working-age population will form an increasingly large proportion of the population, creating a window for a demographic dividend. However, the widening upper sections of the projected population pyramid also point to a steadily growing elderly population by 2036, signalling the need to simultaneously invest in employment and skills for the working-age population while strengthening systems for ageing, healthcare and social security.

**Health and nutrition.** Angul’s health and nutrition landscape reflects a pattern of gradual progress alongside emerging vulnerabilities. While the district’s health infrastructure provides a basic network of 33 Primary Health Centres, 9 Community Health Centres and 166 Health Sub Centres, the availability of just 31 beds per 1,00,000 population points to limited institutional capacity for a district of its size. Nutritional outcomes have improved in some respects, with stunting and underweight among children declining between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5. However, the rise in wasting suggests that acute malnutrition remains a persistent concern. Anaemia among young children and pregnant women rose over the same period, which makes micronutrient nutrition the clearest next area of focus. Combined with an estimated Maternal Mortality Ratio of 197 during 2017–19, these trends indicate that improvements in general nutrition have not translated uniformly into better maternal and micronutrient health, making anaemia reduction, maternal care and strengthened health-system capacity critical priorities for the district.

**Education.** Angul’s education profile reflects a relatively strong foundation in access and institutional capacity, but with persistent challenges in equity, digital preparedness and retention. Manageable pupil-teacher ratios at the Middle and Secondary levels suggest that classroom capacity is broadly adequate, while high enrolment and transition rates indicate that most children successfully enter and move through the school system. The next step is to carry this progress into the secondary years, where the dropout rate has risen and keeping students in school can add the most. The district also continues to face a substantial gender gap in literacy, with female literacy trailing male literacy by more than 17 percentage points. At the same time, uneven digital infrastructure—with only around one-fifth of schools equipped with functional smart classrooms despite wider computer availability—highlights the need to modernise learning environments. Going forward, Angul’s education challenge will be less about expanding basic access and more about ensuring that students, particularly girls and those at risk of dropping out, remain in school and have access to quality, technology-enabled learning opportunities.

**Geography.** Angul district sits at the geographic heart of Odisha, occupying roughly 6,232–6,375 sq km (sources vary slightly) between 20°31′N–21°40′N latitude and 84°15′E–85°23′E longitude, with elevation ranging from about 195 m at the district headquarters to 1,187 m at Malayagiri, its highest point. The district is bounded by two of Odisha’s major rivers, with the Mahanadi flowing along its southern edge and the Brahmani along the north, and its terrain is a mix of plateau land, rolling hills, and fertile river valleys. In the south, the Eastern Ghats give rise to the dramatic Satkosia Gorge, while the north grows more rugged with the Malyagiri mountain range. The Mahanadi itself carves a roughly 22-km narrow gorge through the district, popularly known as Satkosia, which serves as a habitat for various crocodile species. Administratively bordered by Cuttack, Sundaragada, Kendujhar, Sambalpur, Debagada, Dhenkanal, Nayagada, and Boudh districts, Angul’s forest cover stood at about 43.51% of its geographical area as of 2023, and this landscape diversity is what allows the district to host both large-scale coal mining operations and substantial untouched forest tracts within the same boundaries.

**Demography.** Balasore is undergoing a clear demographic transition, with population growth gradually slowing as fertility declines and the age structure matures. The district is moving away from a predominantly youthful population towards one characterised by a larger working-age population and a steadily growing elderly population. While this creates an important window for harnessing the demographic dividend, the gradual rise in population ageing will also increase the need for stronger health, social protection and elderly care systems. Limited urbanisation suggests that much of this demographic transition will continue to unfold within a predominantly rural context, while the improving sex ratio indicates a gradual movement towards greater demographic balance.

**Health and nutrition.** Balasore's health profile reflects steady improvements in child survival and nutritional outcomes, supported by an extensive primary healthcare network. Declining mortality and reductions in stunting, wasting and underweight suggest progress in maternal and child health; however, these gains are tempered by persistent challenges in healthcare capacity and maternal health. Anaemia has emerged as a particularly significant concern, especially among children, indicating that improvements in overall nutrition have not necessarily translated into better micronutrient outcomes. Going forward, strengthening healthcare access, addressing maternal health risks and adopting more targeted interventions against anaemia will be critical to sustaining the district's broader health gains.

**Education.** Balasore's education system is characterised by extensive school access and strong student progression through the foundational and middle stages, supported by a predominantly government-led network and relatively favourable teacher availability. The next opportunity is to turn these gains into completed schooling, especially at the secondary level, where keeping more students enrolled would add the most. Gender disparities in literacy also remain significant, while uneven digital infrastructure limits the wider integration of technology into learning. Overall, the district has established a strong base for universal access and progression, but improving secondary-level retention, reducing gender gaps and strengthening digital learning facilities will be critical to improving educational outcomes.

**Geography.** Balasore, on Odisha's northernmost coast (3,634 sq km), splits into three zones: a sandy, brackish-water coastal belt (~83 km) unsuitable for cultivation, a fertile inner deltaic alluvial plain, and northwestern hills, drained by the Budhabalanga and Subarnarekha rivers. It borders West Bengal's Medinipur to the north, the Bay of Bengal to the east, Bhadrak to the south, and Mayurbhanj/Kendujhar to the west. Key places of interest include Chandipur Beach, the Nilagiri Palace, and the Emami Jagannath and Khirachora Gopinatha temples. Balasore is highly cyclone- and flood-prone, repeatedly hit by cyclones (Yaas, and recent 2025 flooding alongside Mayurbhanj and Jajpur) with the Subarnarekha and Budhabalanga regularly breaching danger levels, worsened by water releases from Jharkhand's dams. Agriculturally, known as the "Granary of Odisha," fertile alluvial and sandy-loam soils support extensive paddy cultivation, alongside coconut, betel, salt manufacturing, and shrimp farming along the coast.

**Demography.** Bargarh is undergoing a gradual demographic transition while retaining its predominantly rural character. With a population of 14.81 lakh and tribal communities accounting for nearly one-fifth of its population, the district's demographic profile is shaped by significant social and cultural diversity. A relatively favourable sex ratio of 977 females per 1,000 males and life expectancy exceeding 75 years for both men and women point towards comparatively positive demographic and health outcomes. At the same time, limited urbanisation, with only 10.13% of the population living in urban areas, highlights the continued importance of agriculture and rural livelihoods in shaping the district's development trajectory. Longer-term trends in population growth, declining fertility and the changing age structure suggest that Bargarh is moving towards lower population growth and an increasingly large working-age population, while the share of children gradually declines and the elderly population expands. This emerging demographic structure presents an opportunity to harness a demographic dividend, but will also require greater attention to productive employment, skills development and the growing social and healthcare needs of an ageing population.

**Health and nutrition.** Bargarh's health and nutrition profile reflects notable gains in child survival and several nutrition outcomes; expanding healthcare capacity and reducing anaemia are the next areas of focus. While its network of health facilities provides a broad service base, low bed availability points to constraints in institutional capacity. Declining neonatal and infant mortality, alongside improvements in wasting and underweight, indicate progress in child health and nutrition, although largely unchanged stunting suggests that chronic malnutrition remains a concern. Anaemia continues to affect a substantial share of young children and pregnant women despite some improvement, highlighting the need for sustained nutrition interventions. With maternal mortality also remaining a concern, the district's priorities should focus on consolidating gains in child survival while strengthening maternal healthcare, reducing anaemia, and addressing the underlying drivers of chronic malnutrition.

**Education.** Bargarh's education landscape reflects a system that has largely succeeded in ensuring access to schooling and maintaining student progression through the foundational and middle years. However, the key challenge emerges at the secondary stage, where retention becomes more difficult and students are more likely to leave the system. Gender disparities in educational attainment also remain a concern, alongside uneven adoption of digital learning infrastructure. Overall, the district has a strong foundation in school access and transition, but greater attention is needed to sustain students through secondary education and ensure more equitable learning opportunities.

**Geography.** Bargarh district lies in the westernmost corner of Odisha, spanning approximately 5,837 sq km between 20°43′–21°41′N latitude and 82°39′–83°58′E longitude, and is bordered by Chhattisgarh to the north and west, Sambalpur district to the east, and Balangir and Subarnapur districts to the south. The major rivers in the district are tributaries of the Mahanadi, with the Jira and Jhaun rivers flowing through Bargarh before joining the Mahanadi in its extreme south, while the Jira's main tributary, the Danta, merges with it near the village Gandturum in Bheden. The district's terrain encompasses fertile plains, forested hills, and river valleys, and is administratively divided into the Bargarh Plain, Borasambar, and Ambabhona and Lakhanpur regions, with the town of Bargarh itself situated on the left bank of the Jira River. This landscape, shaped significantly by the Hirakud Dam project's canal network passing through the region, supports the district's predominantly agrarian economy centered on rice, pulses, and sugarcane cultivation.

**Demography.** Bhadrak is progressing through an advanced demographic transition marked by slowing population growth, declining fertility and a gradual shift towards an older age structure. The shrinking share of children and the expansion of the working-age population create an important opportunity to harness a demographic dividend, although this window is likely to narrow as the elderly population grows. The district's future development will therefore need to balance investments in education, skills and employment for its working-age population with strengthening healthcare, social security and care systems for an increasingly ageing society. Limited urbanisation also suggests that these demographic changes will continue to shape development largely within a predominantly rural setting, while the improving sex ratio points towards a gradual movement towards greater demographic balance.

**Health and nutrition.** Bhadrak's health profile presents a mixed picture of progress and persistent nutritional challenges. While improvements in child survival and relatively better maternal health outcomes suggest gains in healthcare delivery, progress in reducing undernutrition has remained limited. Alongside the improvements in mortality, anaemia rose among both children and pregnant women, so micronutrient nutrition is the main area for the next round of attention. Strengthening primary healthcare, maternal and child nutrition services, and targeted interventions to prevent and treat anaemia will therefore be central to improving the district's overall health outcomes.

**Education.** Bhadrak's education system reflects strong access and progression, supported by a predominantly government-led school network and favourable pupil-teacher ratios at the middle stage. Enrolment remains high through the primary and upper-primary years, while transition rates indicate that most students successfully move between successive stages of schooling. However, retention emerges as a greater challenge at the secondary level, where dropout becomes significantly more pronounced. The district also continues to face a gender gap in literacy and uneven digital readiness, with access to computers considerably stronger than the availability of smart classrooms. Overall, Bhadrak has established a strong foundation for educational access and progression, but improving secondary retention, reducing gender disparities and strengthening digital learning infrastructure remain important priorities.

**Geography.** Bhadrak, in Odisha's coastal plains, is divided into salt tracks along the coast (not arable) and a fertile arable tract known as the "granary" of this part of the state, with soils split across saline, alluvial, and sandy zones; deltaic rivers including the Salandi, Baitarani, Kansabansa, Gamol, Mantei, Genguti, and Kochila flow through the district. It borders Baleshwar to the north, Kendujhar to the west, the Baitarani River and Jajpur to the south, and the Bay of Bengal and Kendrapada to the east. Key places of interest include the Bhadrakali Temple on the Salandi's banks and Bhitarkanika's edge near Basudebpur. Coastal exposure makes Bhadrak vulnerable to cyclones and flooding from the Salandi and Baitarani, with floods known to travel several kilometres inland and damage standing crops, prompting reliance on weirs and canals for dry-season water management. Agriculturally, paddy is the principal crop, followed by other cereals, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables, spices, and sugarcane.

**Demography.** Balangir's demographic profile reflects a district undergoing a steady demographic transition while retaining its predominantly rural character. Population growth has moderated alongside declining fertility, and improvements in life expectancy point to gradual gains in health and survival. The district is entering a favourable phase with a growing working-age population, offering an opportunity to accelerate economic growth and improve livelihoods before population ageing becomes more pronounced. Despite a relatively balanced sex ratio and modest urbanization, much of Balangir's population continues to reside in rural areas, where access to quality education, healthcare, and employment remains uneven. Together, these trends position the district at a critical juncture, where investments in human capital, rural development, and inclusive economic opportunities will determine how effectively it can translate its demographic dividend into long-term development.

**Health and nutrition.** Balangir has made steady progress in improving maternal and child health, with reductions in child mortality and improvements in several nutrition indicators reflecting better access to essential health and nutrition services. However, the district continues to face significant challenges. Healthcare infrastructure remains limited relative to the needs of its largely rural population, while high levels of anaemia among children and women continue to pose a major public health concern. Although chronic undernutrition has declined, persistent micronutrient deficiencies and gaps in healthcare access underscore the need for sustained investments in preventive healthcare, nutrition interventions, and strengthening primary healthcare systems to improve overall health outcomes.

**Education.** Balangir has made notable progress in expanding access to education, with high enrolment at the elementary level and strong transition rates between preparatory, middle and secondary stages. However, learning continuity remains a challenge, as dropout rates increase significantly at the secondary level, particularly among vulnerable groups. The district's education system is predominantly government-run, supported by favourable pupil-teacher ratios that provide a conducive learning environment. At the same time, gaps in digital infrastructure persist, with only a limited proportion of schools equipped with functional smart classrooms, highlighting the need for greater investment in technology-enabled learning and improved educational infrastructure to enhance learning outcomes and retention.

**Geography.** Balangir, in western Odisha's undulating heartland (6,575 sq km), is part of the drought-prone KBK region, with rolling hills, forests, and hill streams draining toward the Mahanadi system, flanked in the northwest by the Gandhamardan hills. It borders Baragada to the north, Subarnapur to the east, Kalahandi to the south, and Nuapada to the west. Key places of interest include the Harishankar Temple in the Gandhamardan hills, the rock-cut temples at Ranipur-Jharial, Gaikhai reservoir, Bhima Dunguri, and Patnagarh, seat of the erstwhile Patna kingdom. Balangir is one of Odisha's most chronically drought-affected, officially recognized districts, with erratic, limited rainfall (~1,215-1,444 mm annually) historically driving large-scale seasonal out-migration; parts also face flash flooding from hill streams. Agriculturally, over 70% of the population depends on farming, with paddy dominant (~61% of gross cropped area), though rainfed cultivation and limited irrigation keep the district vulnerable to monsoon variability.

**Demography.** Boudh is undergoing a clear demographic transition, marked by slowing population growth, declining fertility and a steadily changing age structure. With a population of 4.41 lakh in 2011, projected to reach 5.52 lakh by 2036, the district remains overwhelmingly rural, with only 4.63% of its population living in urban areas, while tribal communities account for 12.55% of the population. Fertility has already fallen below replacement level and is projected to decline further, contributing to a sharp reduction in the share of children and a corresponding expansion of the working-age population. By 2036, this could strengthen the district's demographic dividend, with the 15–59 age group accounting for nearly two-thirds of the population. At the same time, the growing share of older persons and the projected recovery in the sex ratio to above 1,000 females per 1,000 males signal an increasingly mature demographic profile. The transition from a broad-based population pyramid towards a more constricted and ageing structure will require Boudh to simultaneously focus on creating productive opportunities for its working-age population while preparing healthcare, social security and support systems for an expanding elderly population.

**Health and nutrition.** Boudh's health and nutrition trajectory reflects steady progress, though important vulnerabilities persist beneath these improvements. Between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5, the district recorded consistent declines in neonatal, infant and under-five mortality, indicating gradual improvements in child survival, while reductions in stunting, wasting and underweight prevalence suggest a broader improvement in nutritional outcomes. The decline in anaemia among pregnant women is another encouraging sign, although the estimated maternal mortality ratio of 81 indicates that maternal health remains an area requiring sustained attention. The district's health infrastructure, comprising 12 Primary Health Centres, 5 Community Health Centres and 67 Health Sub Centres, with 35 beds per 1,00,000 population, provides the foundation for service delivery but will need to respond to these continuing challenges. Anaemia among children aged 6–59 months rose from 44.1% to 56.2%, which makes micronutrient nutrition the area where further effort can do the most. Boudh's priority, therefore, is to consolidate gains in child and maternal health while strengthening early childhood nutrition and anaemia interventions to ensure that improvements in overall health outcomes are more evenly sustained.

**Education.** Boudh's education system has achieved broad access and strong progression through the early stages of schooling, supported by a predominantly government-led school network and relatively adequate teacher availability at the middle level. However, the district faces a significant challenge in retaining students at the secondary stage, where dropout rises sharply despite strong transition rates between stages. A substantial gender gap in literacy also points to persistent inequalities in educational attainment, while digital infrastructure remains uneven, with access to computers considerably stronger than the availability of smart classrooms. Overall, the key priority for Boudh is to translate strong early-stage enrolment and progression into sustained participation and completion at the secondary level, while addressing gender disparities and strengthening digital learning infrastructure.

**Geography.** Boudh, in central Odisha, is bounded by the Mahanadi River and Anugola to the north, Kandhamala to the south, Nayagada to the east, and the Tel River and Subarnapur to the west. Forest cover is dominated by Sal, Sisal, Bija, Asana, and Mahua species, with the Bagh river, a perennial tributary of the Mahanadi, flowing through the district. Key places of interest include the Satkosia Gorge crocodile sanctuary at Tikarpada. Collection of minor forest produce — Kendu leaf, tamarind, mahua flower and seeds, sal seeds — is a major livelihood source for the district's population, and drought mitigation in its rainfed tracts emphasizes in-situ rainwater conservation and on-farm reservoirs to capture local runoff and flash-flood water. Agriculturally, paddy, pulses, and vegetable cultivation dominate the fertile riverine plains, sustained by the district's rich network of streams and Mahanadi tributaries.

**Demography.** Cuttack is undergoing an advanced demographic transition characterised by slowing population growth, very low fertility and a steadily ageing population. Its relatively high level of urbanisation and longer life expectancy distinguish it from many of Odisha's more rural districts, while the declining share of children and sustained dominance of the working-age population continue to provide an opportunity to harness the demographic dividend. However, this window is likely to narrow as the elderly population expands rapidly, creating growing demand for healthcare, social protection and long-term care. The district's improving sex ratio also indicates a gradual movement towards greater demographic balance, although its future development will increasingly need to adapt to the economic and social implications of an ageing population.

**Health and nutrition.** Cuttack's health profile reflects a relatively well-developed healthcare system and improving survival outcomes, supported by a broad network of health facilities. However, these gains have not translated into comparable improvements in nutrition. Child undernutrition remains a concern, with signs of worsening stunting, wasting and underweight, while childhood anaemia has emerged as a particularly serious challenge. The district therefore presents a contrasting picture: stronger healthcare capacity and declining mortality coexist with persistent nutritional vulnerabilities, highlighting the need to complement curative and maternal-child health services with greater emphasis on nutrition, prevention and early childhood interventions.

**Education.** Cuttack's education system is extensive and predominantly government-led, supported by relatively favourable teacher availability and strong enrolment and transition outcomes. While access and retention remain broadly robust through the primary and middle stages, some students continue to be lost as they progress to secondary education, indicating the need for greater attention to retention at higher grades. The district also shows considerable progress in educational attainment, with literacy levels substantially higher than in less-developed districts, although a persistent gender gap highlights the need for continued efforts to strengthen girls' educational participation and outcomes. Overall, Cuttack combines a large and established school network with comparatively strong access, retention and literacy, while the key challenge lies in sustaining these gains through the secondary stage and narrowing remaining gender disparities.

**Geography.** Cuttack, located in the eastern part of Odisha, sits at the head of the Mahanadi delta and covers about 3,932 sq km of predominantly flat, low-lying deltaic terrain intersected by numerous active and abandoned river channels — apart from a stretch of broken hill country in its Athagarh and Banki subdivisions on either side of the Mahanadi. The district is bordered by Anugola, Dhenkanal, and Jajpur to the north, Kendrapada and Jagatsinghapur to the east, and Puri and Khordha to the south and west. Key places of interest include Barabati Fort and Stadium in Cuttack city, the freshwater Ansupa Lake near Banki, Deojhar Waterfall, and the Bhattarika and Chandikhole temples. Being deltaic and criss-crossed by the Mahanadi and Kathajodi rivers, Cuttack is highly flood-prone, with land often waterlogged during the monsoon and a reliance on an extensive network of embankments, canals, and weirs for flood control and irrigation; farmers here are noted to have comparatively lower adaptive capacity to climate shocks than some neighbouring coastal districts. Agriculturally, paddy is the dominant crop, cultivated nearly year-round owing to fertile alluvial soils and canal irrigation, with villages traditionally built on raised artificial ground with tanks (pokharis) to cope with the seasonally waterlogged plains.

**Demography.** Debagarh is a predominantly rural and tribal district undergoing a significant demographic transition. Its large tribal population, including the Paudi Bhuyan PVTG, remains central to the district's social and cultural composition. Population growth has slowed considerably alongside a sharp decline in fertility, signalling a shift away from the district's earlier phase of rapid demographic expansion. At the same time, the age structure is changing: the working-age population has expanded, creating a potential demographic opportunity, while the share of children is steadily declining and the elderly population is projected to grow substantially. Improving life expectancy and a gradually recovering sex ratio further reflect broader improvements in demographic outcomes. Together, these trends suggest that Debagarh is moving toward a more mature population structure, where the immediate challenge will be to translate its large working-age population into productive employment while preparing for the growing social and economic demands of an ageing population.

**Health and nutrition.** Debagarh's health profile reflects significant challenges in both healthcare access and population health outcomes. Despite some improvement in child mortality over recent years, neonatal, infant and under-five mortality remain relatively high, while maternal mortality continues to be a serious concern. The district's limited health infrastructure and low bed availability further underline the need to strengthen access to essential healthcare, particularly for mothers and children. Nutritional outcomes present a mixed picture, with some progress in reducing chronic undernutrition and underweight, but worsening levels of wasting indicating persistent acute nutritional stress. Childhood anaemia rose markedly, which makes it a priority for the district's maternal and child health programmes. Overall, Debagarh requires greater emphasis on strengthening primary healthcare, maternal and child health services, and targeted nutrition interventions to address these interconnected challenges.

**Education.** Debagarh's education system is predominantly government-led and benefits from relatively favourable teacher availability and strong transitions across school stages. While enrolment is strong at the primary level, the lower participation at the upper-primary stage points to challenges in sustaining children's engagement as they progress through the system. Transition rates remain high, and dropout is relatively contained through the middle stage but rises noticeably at secondary level, highlighting the need to strengthen retention during adolescence. Literacy outcomes are comparatively better among men, but the substantial gender gap in literacy points to persistent barriers to women's educational attainment. Overall, Debagarh has a strong foundational school network, but improving continuity into higher grades and narrowing gender disparities remain important priorities.

**Geography.** Debagarh, bifurcated from Sambalpur in 1994, is a small, sparsely populated district (2,782 sq km) in northwestern Odisha's Koshal region — hilly and heavily forested, with ranges like Khajuria (up to 745 m) drained by streams such as the Daragadi. It borders Sundaragada to the north, Anugola to the east and south, and Sambalpur to the west. Key places include Padhanpuri waterfall, Deojharan (Kurudkut) waterfall, Gohira Dam, Katasar Ghat's Banadurga temple, and the historic Bamra royal temples in Debagarh town. The district is officially recognized as drought-prone, having been declared drought-affected in recent years alongside Baragada, Balangir, Jharsuguda, and Sambalpur; it also falls within the Maoist-affected Red Corridor. Agriculturally, hilly terrain and low rainfall (~1,014 mm annually) limit irrigation, with paddy concentrated in valley and lowland tracts and much of the population, tribal and non-tribal alike, dependent on rainfed farming and forest livelihoods.

**Demography.** Dhenkanal is a predominantly rural district with a modest tribal presence and a population undergoing a clear demographic transition. Population growth has slowed considerably from its earlier peak, accompanied by a sustained decline in fertility, indicating that the district is moving toward a more stable population trajectory. The age structure reinforces this transition: the working-age population has expanded, creating a window of demographic opportunity, while the share of children is steadily declining and the elderly population is growing rapidly. Although the sex ratio has improved from its earlier low, it remains below parity, highlighting a continuing gender imbalance. Rising life expectancy further reflects improving survival conditions, but also reinforces the emerging need to prepare for population ageing. Overall, Dhenkanal is moving from a relatively youthful population structure toward a more mature one, making employment generation, human capital development and preparation for ageing increasingly important for its future development.

**Health and nutrition.** Dhenkanal's health profile reflects improving survival outcomes alongside persistent and worsening nutritional challenges. The district has a relatively broad primary healthcare network, and mortality indicators have declined substantially, suggesting progress in maternal and child health services. Child nutrition is the area to build on next: stunting, wasting and underweight rose between NFHS-4 and NFHS-5. Anaemia has emerged as the most critical concern, affecting both children and pregnant women and pointing to persistent gaps in nutrition and preventive healthcare. Overall, Dhenkanal's experience highlights a growing disconnect between improvements in healthcare and survival outcomes and the nutritional well-being of vulnerable populations, underscoring the need for stronger, integrated maternal, child and nutrition interventions.

**Education.** Dhenkanal's education system is predominantly government-led and supported by a relatively strong school network, with teacher availability remaining broadly favourable. Access and participation are also encouraging, with high enrolment and strong transition from preparatory to middle and middle to secondary stages. However, the rise in dropout at the secondary level suggests that retaining students through adolescence remains a key challenge. The district has made considerable progress in educational attainment, although a persistent gender gap in literacy indicates that women and girls continue to face disadvantages in educational outcomes. At the same time, the growing availability of digital learning facilities provides an opportunity to strengthen the quality and relevance of education. Overall, Dhenkanal's priority lies less in expanding basic access and more in improving retention, learning continuity and gender equity as students progress to higher levels of schooling.

**Geography.** Dhenkanal, centrally located in Odisha (4,452 sq km), is mainly plains dotted with discontinuous, forested hill ranges along its southern border — known as "Home of Elephants and Tigers" for its dense forest and wildlife. It borders Kendujhar to the north, Jajpur to the east, Kataka to the south, and Anugola to the west. Key places of interest include Kapilash Hill and the Chandrasekhar Mahadev Temple, Buddheswar Temple, and the Mahima Dharma site at Joranda, famous for its Maghamela fair. The district isn't among Odisha's officially notified drought or flood-prone areas, sitting in a comparatively moderate climate zone (~1,421 mm annual rainfall), though its southern hill tracts remain more rain-dependent than the plains. Agriculturally, fertile soils and adequate monsoon rainfall support diverse cropping — paddy is the staple, alongside groundnut, cashew, potato, sugarcane, mango, jackfruit, and vegetables, contributing to a relatively prosperous rural economy.

**Demography.** Gajapati is a predominantly rural and strongly tribal district, with tribal communities forming a central part of its demographic and social character, including the Saora and Lanjia Saora PVTGs. The district is undergoing a marked demographic transition, characterised by steadily slowing population growth and declining fertility. At the same time, its age structure is shifting rapidly, with the working-age population expanding before gradually easing, while the share of children declines and the elderly population grows. A relatively favourable sex ratio and rising life expectancy indicate positive demographic conditions, but the growing elderly population will increasingly require stronger social protection and age-responsive services. Overall, Gajapati is moving from a youthful demographic profile toward a more mature population structure, creating an opportunity to harness its expanding working-age population while ensuring that tribal and rural communities are not left behind in the transition.

**Health and nutrition.** Gajapati's health profile reveals persistent maternal and child health challenges despite a substantial network of primary healthcare facilities. Mortality remains relatively high, particularly among newborns and young children, while maternal mortality continues to be a major concern. Nutrition is the main area for further gains: child nutrition indicators moved the less favourable way, and anaemia rose among both children and pregnant women. Although wasting has shown some improvement, this isolated gain is outweighed by worsening stunting, underweight and anaemia. Stronger primary healthcare, maternal care and targeted nutrition support, especially in rural and tribal communities, can build on these foundations.

**Education.** Gajapati's education system is predominantly government-led, with a broad school network and growing access to digital learning facilities. While primary enrolment is relatively strong, participation declines at the upper-primary stage, and transition becomes a greater challenge as students move toward secondary education. Keeping adolescents in school is the next opportunity: dropout at the secondary level has risen, and transition rates show the work can start in the middle years. Educational attainment remains a major concern, with literacy levels considerably below those of many other districts and a pronounced gender gap. These disadvantages are particularly significant in a district with a large tribal population, underscoring the need for more inclusive and context-specific strategies to improve retention, secondary education and girls' learning outcomes.

**Geography.** Gajapati, in southeastern Odisha (3,850 sq km), lies in the Eastern Ghats and is dominated by rugged, hilly terrain and narrow valleys — over 60% of land is hilly/upland — centered on the Mahendragiri massif and drained by the Mahendratanaya and Vamsadhara rivers. It borders Andhra Pradesh to the south, Ganjam to the east, Rayagada to the west, and Kandhamala to the north. Key places of interest include Mahendragiri hill and temple, Gandahati waterfall, the Buddhist Padmasambhava Mahavihara monastery, and the Gajapati/B.N. Palace at Paralakhemundi, the district headquarters. The district isn't officially drought-notified, but heavy monsoon downpours in the hills can trigger flash flooding in lowland stretches along the Vamsadhara, while rain-shadow pockets and erratic rainfall (~1,403 mm annually, less stable than northern Odisha) leave it periodically drought-prone too. Agriculturally, the hilly terrain and favorable soil/climate support horticulture (its main strength) alongside paddy, sugarcane, sunflower, and oilseeds, with medium and low lands (35% combined) carrying most food-grain cultivation.

**Demography.** Ganjam is one of Odisha's most populous and relatively urbanised districts, with a comparatively modest tribal presence. Its demographic trajectory reflects a clear transition from rapid population growth toward slower expansion, driven by sustained declines in fertility. At the same time, the age structure is becoming progressively older: the working-age population has expanded, while the share of children is falling and the elderly population is increasing steadily. Relatively high life expectancy further reinforces this shift, pointing to longer periods of survival and a growing ageing population. The gradual recovery in the sex ratio is encouraging, although the district continues to face a gender imbalance. Overall, Ganjam is moving toward a mature demographic profile, creating opportunities to harness its large working-age population while increasingly preparing for the economic and social implications of population ageing.

**Health and nutrition.** Ganjam's health profile reflects a relatively extensive healthcare system and improving child survival outcomes, but significant gaps remain in maternal health and nutrition. Despite progress in reducing neonatal, infant and under-five mortality, maternal mortality remains a major concern. Nutritional outcomes are also mixed, with worsening levels of stunting and wasting and little improvement in underweight among children. Anaemia has emerged as the most pressing nutritional challenge, affecting both children and pregnant women at increasingly high levels. Maternal health and nutrition are where stronger maternal care, preventive services and integrated nutrition programmes can add the most across the district.

**Education.** Ganjam's education system is extensive and predominantly government-led, with strong enrolment and transition through the primary and middle stages. However, retention becomes more challenging at the secondary level, where dropout increases noticeably. The district has also expanded access to digital learning infrastructure, creating greater scope for technology-enabled education. Despite these strengths, literacy outcomes reveal a persistent gender gap, with women continuing to lag behind men in educational attainment. Overall, Ganjam has a strong foundation in school access and progression, but improving secondary-level retention and narrowing gender disparities remain key priorities.

**Geography.** Ganjam, in southern coastal Odisha (about 8,206 sq km), combines a coastal plain with hilly Eastern Ghats terrain in its interior, watered by small rivers including the Rushikulya, and home to the Chilika Lake, Asia's largest brackish-water lagoon. It borders the Bay of Bengal to the east, Gajapati to the south, Kandhamala to the west, and Puri/Khordha to the north, with Andhra Pradesh nearby to the south. Key places of interest include Gopalpur beach, Taratarini Temple, Chilika Lake, and Berhampur, the district's commercial and silk-weaving hub. Ganjam is one of Odisha's most cyclone- and flood-vulnerable coastal districts — repeatedly the worst-hit in major cyclones (e.g., Phailin, Titli), with the Rushikulya and Vamsadhara prone to overflowing — while pockets also experience drought stress. Agriculturally, it's a rainfed, flood-prone deltaic tract where paddy dominates (over 80% of cropped area), supplemented by fisheries and salt manufacturing along the coast, with irrigation supported by the Rushikulya Barrage.

**Demography.** Jagatsinghpur's demographic story is one of a district that has largely completed its demographic transition. Rapid population growth of earlier decades has given way to slow growth as fertility has declined to well below replacement levels, fundamentally reshaping the district's age structure. A shrinking child population, a stabilising working-age cohort, and a steadily rising elderly population signal the emergence of an ageing society. Although the district has a very small tribal population and remains only moderately urbanised, its strategic coastal location and industrial significance distinguish it from many other districts in Odisha. Improvements in life expectancy reflect steady gains in health and well-being, while the relatively low sex ratio points to continuing gender imbalances. As Jagatsinghpur moves into a phase of low fertility and population ageing, its future development will increasingly depend on strengthening human capital, supporting an ageing population, and sustaining economic growth through productive employment and resilient social infrastructure.

**Health and nutrition.** Jagatsinghpur has made notable strides in improving maternal and child health, with steady declines in neonatal, infant, and under-five mortality reflecting better survival outcomes. Maternal mortality is also comparatively low, reinforcing the district's strong health profile. Nutritional indicators have improved across the board, with marked reductions in stunting, wasting, and underweight among children. Anaemia rose, particularly among children and pregnant women, making it the district's main public health priority. Supported by an extensive network of primary health centres, community health centres, and health sub-centres, the district has strengthened healthcare access, though limited bed availability suggests room for further expansion. Overall, Jagatsinghpur presents a picture of strong progress in healthcare and nutrition, tempered by the growing challenge of widespread anaemia.

**Education.** Jagatsinghpur's education system reflects the advantages of a district that has largely achieved universal access to schooling. Literacy levels are high, with a relatively narrow gender gap, while enrolment and transition rates remain consistently strong across school stages. Dropout is minimal during the middle years and remains comparatively low at the secondary level, indicating that most students continue their education. A balanced mix of government, aided, and private schools supports the system, complemented by favourable teacher availability and expanding digital infrastructure. While access to computers has improved considerably, the wider adoption of smart classrooms remains an important area for further development.

**Geography.** Jagatsinghpur, Odisha's smallest district (1,759 sq km), is a deltaic and partly littoral coastal tract, triangular in shape, drained by the Mahanadi, Kathajodi, Devi, and Biluakhai rivers. It borders Kendrapada to the north, Puri to the south, the Bay of Bengal to the east, and Kataka to the west. Key places of interest include Paradeep Port and beach, the Maa Sarala Temple, Gorekhnath Temple, and Siali Beach. Being a low-lying coastal delta, Jagatsinghpur is highly vulnerable to floods, cyclones, and occasional drought from erratic rainfall — the 1999 super cyclone caused severe damage here — with saline soils and waterlogging further affecting agriculture in parts. Farming is the mainstay of the economy, with paddy as the principal crop alongside sugarcane, turmeric, cotton, and jute; fisheries and Paradeep's port-linked industries (refinery, fertiliser) also contribute significantly to the local economy.

**Demography.** Jajpur is a predominantly rural district with a modest tribal presence and a population undergoing a steady demographic transition. Its population has expanded substantially over the past century, but growth has slowed considerably alongside a sharp decline in fertility, pointing toward a progressively stabilising population. The sex ratio, after a prolonged historical decline, has begun to recover and is projected to approach parity, while life expectancy has also improved. The age structure is shifting decisively toward maturity: the working-age population expanded to a peak in the early 2020s, while the share of children is declining and the elderly population is rising steadily. With fertility projected to fall further below replacement level, Jajpur is moving from a relatively youthful population toward a low-fertility and ageing structure. This transition presents an opportunity to leverage the expanding working-age population in the near term, while building systems for employment, social protection and elderly care to address the longer-term implications of ageing.

**Health and nutrition.** Jajpur's health profile reflects steady progress in child survival and nutrition, supported by a broad network of primary healthcare facilities, although service capacity remains relatively limited. Maternal and child mortality have declined, indicating improvements in access to and delivery of essential health services. Nutritional outcomes have also strengthened, with reductions in stunting, wasting and underweight among children, suggesting gradual gains in child nutrition. Anaemia rose among both children and pregnant women, making it the district's main nutrition priority. The contrast highlights the need to sustain progress in child nutrition while placing greater emphasis on anaemia prevention, maternal nutrition and integrated primary healthcare.

**Education.** Jajpur's education system has a strong government presence and relatively favourable enrolment and transition outcomes at the elementary level, but challenges become more pronounced as students advance to secondary education. While teacher availability is broadly adequate and most students continue through the middle and secondary stages, the rising dropout rate at the secondary level points to growing retention pressures. A persistent gender gap in literacy, along with limited access to digital learning infrastructure such as smart classrooms, further highlights areas where the district's education system needs greater support to improve equity, continuity, and learning opportunities.

**Geography.** Jajpur, in eastern Odisha (about 2,888 sq km), sits on the coastal plain, with its southern part lying in the Brahmani delta, drained by the Brahmani, Baitarani, and their distributaries (Kharasua, Kelua). It borders Kendujhar and Bhadrak to the north, Kataka to the south, Dhenkanal to the west, and Kendrapada to the east. Key places of interest include the ancient Biraja Temple, Ratnagiri's Buddhist ruins, the Chandikhole hot spring, and the meditating Shiva statue near Jajpur town. Being low-lying and river-fed, Jajpur is flood-prone during the monsoon, with occasional drought stress from erratic rainfall; the district has also become an industrial hub, with the Kalinga Nagar steel cluster raising land-use and environmental pressures alongside agriculture. Agriculturally, the district is largely agrarian, with paddy the dominant crop on the fertile deltaic and coastal plains, supported by moderate rainfall (~1,015-1,757 mm depending on the year) and river irrigation.

**Demography.** Jharsuguda is a relatively urbanised and industrialised district with a substantial tribal presence and a demographic transition that is already well advanced. Population growth has slowed considerably after peaking in the late twentieth century, alongside a sharp decline in fertility to well below replacement level. The district also records relatively high life expectancy, while the sex ratio, after a prolonged historical decline, is gradually recovering toward parity. Its age structure reflects the transition clearly: the working-age population has expanded, the share of children is steadily contracting, and the elderly population is expected to grow substantially. With fertility projected to remain exceptionally low, Jharsuguda is likely to experience an increasingly mature and ageing population. Its higher urbanisation and industrial character may provide greater opportunities to leverage the working-age population, but they also make employment quality, social protection and preparations for population ageing increasingly important.

**Health and nutrition.** Jharsuguda's health profile reflects relatively strong healthcare capacity and improving maternal and child survival outcomes. Its comparatively well-developed health infrastructure is accompanied by declines in neonatal, infant and under-five mortality, while maternal mortality remains lower than in several other districts. Child nutrition has also improved substantially, with reductions in stunting, wasting and underweight prevalence indicating progress in addressing undernutrition. However, persistently high and rising anaemia among young children remains a major concern and represents a key gap in the district's otherwise improving nutrition profile. Overall, Jharsuguda has made encouraging progress in health and child nutrition, but sustained attention to anaemia prevention and maternal and child nutrition is essential to consolidate these gains.

**Education.** Jharsuguda's education system is predominantly government-led and benefits from a relatively strong school infrastructure, favourable teacher availability and extensive access to digital facilities. Enrolment is robust across the primary and upper-primary stages, while transition rates are exceptionally strong through secondary education, indicating effective continuation within the school system. However, the sharp increase in dropout at the secondary stage points to emerging retention challenges during adolescence. Literacy outcomes also reveal a persistent gender gap, with female literacy substantially lower than male literacy. Overall, Jharsuguda combines strong access, transition and digital readiness with the need to improve secondary-level retention and address gender disparities in educational attainment.

**Geography.** Jharsuguda, Odisha's smallest district by population (2,081 sq km), lies in the western rolling uplands, drained by the Ib and Bheden rivers, with hilly, stony terrain in parts and brownish-black soils in the plains. It borders Sundaragada to the north, Sambalpur to the east, Baragada to the south, and Chhattisgarh to the west. Key places of interest include the Koilighugar waterfall, the prehistoric rock paintings of Bikramkhol, and the Shiva shrine at Mahadebpalli. Jharsuguda has been officially declared drought-affected in recent years alongside western neighbours like Baragada, Balangir, and Sambalpur, reflecting periodic monsoon deficits, even as it is Odisha's most mineral-rich, industrially developed and urbanized district, hosting major thermal power and metallurgical plants. Agriculturally, paddy and vegetables are grown in the plains' brownish-black soils, while the hilly, stony tracts limit cultivation, with only a modest share of the district's land under farming compared to its industrial footprint.

**Demography.** Kalahandi's demographic story is one of rapid transformation. Once characterised by sustained population growth and relatively high fertility, the district is now moving swiftly through the demographic transition as family sizes shrink and population growth slows. This shift is gradually reshaping its age structure, with a growing working-age population offering a window of opportunity for economic development even as the share of older persons continues to rise. Although tribal communities remain an important part of the district's social fabric, Kalahandi's demographic profile is more diverse than many neighbouring districts. Improvements in the sex ratio and life expectancy reflect steady gains in health and well-being, while the district's predominantly rural character and limited urbanization continue to influence access to services and livelihoods. As Kalahandi transitions towards a more mature population structure, its long-term development will depend on effectively harnessing its demographic dividend while preparing for the challenges of an ageing population.

**Health and nutrition.** Kalahandi's health and nutrition landscape reflects a district where progress in healthcare delivery has begun to translate into better outcomes, but significant gaps remain. Expanded health infrastructure and improved access to services have contributed to reductions in child mortality and a steady decline in multiple forms of child undernutrition, signalling gradual improvements in maternal and child health. Despite these gains, neonatal survival continues to be a major concern, pointing to the need for stronger antenatal, delivery, and newborn care. Anaemia also remains deeply entrenched among women and children, limiting overall health gains and highlighting persistent nutritional deficiencies. Going forward, improving the quality of maternal and newborn care, strengthening nutrition programmes, and expanding preventive healthcare will be essential to sustaining progress and reducing avoidable health disparities across the district.

**Education.** Kalahandi's education sector reflects steady progress in expanding access and improving student retention, making it one of the stronger-performing districts in the region. High enrolment at the elementary level and strong transition rates into secondary education indicate that most children are able to remain in the school system through the foundational years. Government schools continue to anchor educational provision, complemented by a growing presence of private institutions, while favourable pupil-teacher ratios and expanding digital infrastructure have strengthened the learning environment. However, a substantial gender gap in literacy persists, highlighting continuing disparities in educational attainment between men and women. Bridging this gap, while further improving the quality of teaching and expanding access to technology-enabled learning, will be key to ensuring more equitable and inclusive educational outcomes.

**Geography.** Kalahandi, in southwestern Odisha (7,920 sq km), is a mix of fertile plains, forested hills, and river valleys, situated on the confluence of the Tel and Uttei rivers with the Indravati also flowing through it, all tributaries of the Mahanadi. It borders Balangir and Nuapada to the north, Nabarangpur, Koraput, and Rayagada to the south, and Rayagada/Kandhamala/Boudh to the east. Key places of interest include the Manikeswari Temple in Bhawanipatna, Karlapat Wildlife Sanctuary, Phurlijharan waterfall, and the Gudahandi rock-art caves. Historically synonymous with drought and famine, Kalahandi remains one of Odisha's officially recognized drought-prone districts with a dry, extreme climate (~1,378 mm annual rainfall), though the Indravati Irrigation Project has since enabled two crops a year across southern blocks, easing some vulnerability. Agriculturally, paddy dominates in irrigated pockets (Kalampur, Junagarh, Dharmagarh), cotton is grown around Kesinga and Bhawanipatna, and forest produce (mahua, kendu leaf, timber, bamboo) remains a significant livelihood source.

**Demography.** Kandhamal is a predominantly rural, tribal and hill-based district, with tribal communities forming the majority of its population and shaping its distinctive demographic character. Unlike many other districts, its sex ratio remains consistently female-favourable, while life expectancy has also improved. The district is, however, progressing more gradually through the demographic transition than more urbanised districts. Fertility remains comparatively high, and the population retains a relatively youthful age structure despite a steady expansion of the working-age population. At the same time, the share of children is declining and the elderly population is gradually increasing, signalling the beginning of a longer-term shift toward population ageing. Overall, Kandhamal combines a youthful demographic base with emerging ageing trends, creating an important opportunity to harness its expanding working-age population while ensuring that rural and tribal communities benefit equitably from improvements in human development and social services.

**Health and nutrition.** Kandhamal's health profile reflects a strong physical health infrastructure, but persistent gaps in access and outcomes, particularly for mothers and children. Despite relatively extensive health facilities and high bed availability, mortality remains elevated, although neonatal, infant and under-five mortality have improved. Maternal health is a particularly serious concern, reflecting the challenges of delivering services across hilly terrain and dispersed tribal communities. Nutrition outcomes are mixed, with some reduction in stunting and underweight, but wasting remains persistently high. Anaemia has worsened among both children and pregnant women, emerging as a major nutritional challenge. Overall, Kandhamal's experience highlights that infrastructure alone is insufficient, with geographic accessibility, quality of maternal care and targeted nutrition interventions remaining critical priorities.

**Education.** Kandhamal's education system is overwhelmingly government-led, with strong elementary-level access and relatively broad digital infrastructure. However, challenges become more pronounced as students progress through the school system. More teachers at the secondary stage, and support during the move to secondary school, are where the next gains lie. Literacy outcomes also reveal a pronounced gender disparity, particularly affecting women and girls. With strong elementary enrolment in place, keeping students in school through adolescence is the key next step. Given the district's predominantly rural, hilly and tribal character, improving accessibility, secondary-stage retention and girls' educational attainment will be central to strengthening educational outcomes.

**Geography.** Kandhamal, in central Odisha (~7,654 sq km), lies in a high-altitude zone dominated by hilly ranges and narrow valleys, with roughly 71% forest cover; it borders Boudh to the north, Rayagada and Gajapati to the south, Ganjam and Nayagada to the east, and Kalahandi to the west. Key places of interest include the hill station of Daringbadi, Baliguda, and scenic spots like Belaghara and Jalespatta. The district isn't formally flood-notified but faces recurring monsoon-driven landslide/flood risk in its steep terrain alongside periodic drought stress from its erratic, monsoon-dependent rainfall (~1,523 mm annually) and acidic, low-fertility red laterite soils prone to erosion. Agriculturally, cultivable land is limited (~12% of area), with paddy, maize, and niger as the main Kharif crops, potato, vegetables, and mustard grown where irrigated, and the district known for its GI-tagged Kandhamal Haldi (turmeric) alongside broader forest-based livelihoods.

**Demography.** Kendrapara is a predominantly rural and agrarian district with a very small tribal population and a demographic profile characterised by relatively favourable gender outcomes. Population growth has slowed considerably from its earlier peak, while the sex ratio remains above parity and is projected to improve further. Fertility, however, remains comparatively high and is expected to decline only gradually, indicating a slower pace of demographic transition than in more urbanised districts. The age structure reflects this gradual shift, with the working-age population forming the largest share, the proportion of children steadily declining, and the elderly population expanding. Overall, Kendrapara retains a relatively young and balanced population structure while gradually moving toward ageing, creating an opportunity to leverage its working-age population while preparing for rising demand for elderly support and social services.

**Health and nutrition.** Kendrapara's health profile reflects gradual improvements in maternal and child survival, but persistent nutritional challenges. While mortality outcomes have improved, they remain relatively high, suggesting continuing gaps in maternal and child healthcare. Nutrition outcomes are mixed: wasting and underweight have declined, but stunting has shown little progress and remains a concern. Anaemia rose among both children and pregnant women, which makes maternal and child nutrition the main area for further gains. Overall, Kendrapara can consolidate its gains in survival by strengthening preventive care and targeted nutrition, especially to bring anaemia down.

**Education.** Kendrapara's education profile reflects strong foundational enrolment and comparatively high literacy, but significant retention challenges emerge at the secondary stage. Elementary enrolment and transition rates remain high and teacher availability is broadly favourable; the next opportunity is at the secondary level, where dropout has risen. The district also retains a predominantly government-led school system and has comparatively strong access to functional computer facilities, although the limited spread of smart classrooms highlights continuing gaps in digital learning infrastructure. A persistent gender gap in literacy further underscores the need to strengthen educational outcomes and retention, particularly for girls as they move into higher stages of schooling.

**Geography.** Kendrapara, in the eastern coastal plain of Odisha (~2,644 sq km), is a low-lying delta and coastal district drained by the Brahmani, Baitarani, and Chitroptala rivers, with a 48-km Bay of Bengal coastline and the ecologically significant Bhitarkanika mangroves and Gahirmatha turtle nesting beach. It borders Bhadrak to the north, Jajpur to the northwest, Jagatsinghapur to the south, and Kataka to the west. Key places of interest include Bhitarkanika Wildlife Sanctuary, Kanika Palace, the Baladevjew Temple, Dangamal, and Pentha and Gahirmatha beaches. Kendrapara lies directly in the path of coastal cyclonic storms and is highly flood- and cyclone-prone (severely hit by cyclones Dana and the 1999 Super Cyclone), with substantial land also classified as saline, waterlogged, and drought-prone. Agriculturally, over 70% of residents depend on farming; rice is the staple crop, alongside groundnut, green/black gram, and jute, though recurring cyclones, floods, and drought regularly disrupt cultivation and livelihoods.

**Demography.** Kendujhar's demographic profile is shaped by its large tribal population, which forms nearly half of the district's residents and strongly influences its social, cultural, and economic character. The district has experienced a gradual demographic transition, with declining fertility leading to slower population growth and an expanding working-age population. A relatively balanced sex ratio and improving life expectancy reflect steady gains in health and survival outcomes, while the gradual rise in the elderly population signals the onset of population ageing. Together, these trends place Kendujhar at an important demographic juncture, offering the potential to harness its demographic dividend while preparing for the long-term challenges of an ageing population.

**Health and nutrition.** Kendujhar's health and nutrition profile reflects both encouraging progress and persistent public health challenges. Maternal and child mortality have declined over time, indicating improvements in healthcare delivery, while a relatively low maternal mortality ratio points to better maternal care. The district's network of primary health centres, community health centres, and sub-centres has expanded access to basic healthcare, although limited hospital bed availability continues to place pressure on health services. Nutrition outcomes present a mixed picture: chronic child undernutrition has improved, but acute malnutrition, underweight prevalence, and anaemia among children and women remain widespread, highlighting persistent deficiencies in dietary diversity and micronutrient intake. These challenges suggest that while healthcare access has steadily improved, strengthening nutrition interventions, preventive healthcare, and health infrastructure remains essential for achieving better health outcomes across the district.

**Education.** Kendujhar's education sector has made significant progress in expanding access to schooling, supported by a strong network of government schools that continue to serve the vast majority of students. Enrolment at the primary level remains high and transition rates between school stages are encouraging, reflecting improved retention through the elementary years. However, dropout rates rise noticeably at the secondary level, indicating challenges in sustaining participation beyond compulsory education. Despite favourable pupil-teacher ratios and growing access to digital infrastructure such as computer facilities and smart classrooms, a substantial gender gap in literacy persists, with women continuing to lag behind men. Overall, Kendujhar's education system has established a solid foundation in access and infrastructure, but improving gender equity, reducing secondary school dropout, and enhancing the quality of learning remain key priorities.

**Geography.** Kendujhar, in northern Odisha (8,303 sq km), lies on an upland plateau within the Keonjhar rolling upland, bordered by low hills to the west and south, part of the Baitarani River basin; home to some of the planet's oldest rock formations (4.2 billion years, at Champua). It borders Jharkhand's West Singhbhum to the north, Mayurbhanj and Bhadrak to the east, Jajpur to the south, and Dhenkanal/Sundaragada to the west. Key places of interest include Sanaghagara and Badaghagara waterfalls, the partial Khandadhar Falls, and the Maa Tarini Temple at Ghatgaon. Kendujhar isn't among Odisha's officially notified drought or flood-prone districts, though its hilly, forested terrain and heavy mining activity create localized environmental stress. Agriculturally, rice is the principal crop, supplemented by maize, til, niger, and arhar, though much arable land remains uncultivated; the district's economy leans heavily on mineral extraction (iron ore, manganese, chromite) and associated industry rather than farming alone.
